item.title: Noir-CKB: the private tally is live on CKB testnet, try it yourself (3 posts)
item.description: Hi Patrick, I didn’t know VoteSecure existed, and it’s really cool to find someone who’s been working on private voting on CKB this long. I’m going to read the v2.3 spec properly this week. Dropping drand for threshold decryption is the right call, I think. I hadn’t thought about the problem where the person generating the key could just look before the release round, and once you see it, you can’t really unsee it. Same with the live totals. Decrypting a running sum twice and getting the votes in between is the kind of leak I would have walked straight into. I did notice something about the batching that might bite you though. One Groth16 verification costs about 117M cycles in my tests,...

item.title: Twine: Buy and Sell CKB Without Depositing on an Exchange (Fiber P2P PoC) (2 posts)
item.description: Great, the fixes are a clear improvement. Two areas I’d still check: If the route disappears after the bank transfer, fiat-sent can be rejected before recording the buyer’s report. Could you preserve that report and handle the routing failure separately? Could the timing calculations follow the actual incoming channel delay and the buyer invoice’s required lock time? The fixed claim margin assumes default channel settings, while the published deadlines assume the shortest invoice lock. That can leave less usable time than the seller and arbitrator windows suggest. These would be useful cases to test with real Fiber nodes. Good progress, and thanks for following the review through. item.title: Living Passport: repair history for phones and laptops on CKB (testnet) (1 posts)
item.description: Hi everyone I’m Anthony, building on the CKB Builder Track. For the last few weeks I’ve been working on Living Passport, a service history for phones and laptops that lives on CKB. The problem When you buy a used phone or laptop, you rely on what the seller tells you about repairs. Repair shops here mostly don’t keep records either, they rely on what the owner says. How it works Each device gets a passport, a cell on CKB with its history in the cell data The shop registers the device at intake from its own wallet, so the customer doesn’t need a wallet or a smartphone The shop records repairs and gives the customer a QR card. item.title: Tranfr — Programmable Recovery for CKB (2 posts)
item.description: Update: capacity rule built, tested, and run on testnet @Hanssen thanks for the capacity feedback. I went with option 1 (branch on type script), with no new args. What changed On a recipient claim, if a Tranfr input carries a type script (e.g. a UDT), the owner-locked outputs must return at least that input’s capacity. Plain CKB cells are unchanged: the recipient takes everything. The owner path is untouched. The lock args stay at 72 bytes (full 32-byte hashes), so the minimum cell capacity is 113 CKB. I kept the full-length hashes for the larger collision margin. If you’d prefer 20-byte hashes to lower the occupation, say so and I’ll switch. Verification The Rust tests cover typed claims...

item.title: Ward: lock proof for CKB (3 posts)
item.description: image1920×1080 357 KB On CKB a lock is a program, so “prove this wallet is mine” has no single answer. A secp256k1 key, a JoyID passkey, a multisig, Omnilock in one of its modes and a smart-account lock each prove control a different way, and a site that wants to check one has to write code for each. Ward gives them one answer. The wallet signs a transaction that can never be committed. The verifier rebuilds that transaction itself, reads the lock’s cell deps from the chain, and runs the lock in CKB-VM. Exit 0 means the wallet controls the lock. One verifier handles every lock that signs the transaction hash, and any wallet that can sign an ordinary transaction can sign the proof, with no...

item.title: Spark Program | Forecast Arena - A Pilot for Honest AI Benchmarks on CKB (1 posts)
item.description: 1. Project overview Forecast Arena is a pilot case for exploring how blockchain can help keep AI benchmarks honest. The project uses a small forecasting benchmark to test whether CKB can preserve an independently verifiable record of the announced trials, evaluation rules, predictions, outcomes, and scores. Two AI agents will commit sealed predictions, reveal them before observation begins, and receive scores calculated from public CKB evidence. A separate verification tool will allow reviewers to check the experiment even when the arena website or backend is unavailable. The central research question is: Can blockchain make changes, omissions, and misreporting in an AI benchmark harder...
